turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yeah, thank you for seeing me. Um, so I'm here because... well, honestly, it's just a lot right now. I came in because I feel like I absolutely cannot get my schoolwork and my little accessories shop organized at the same time. 

I started this shop online recently, just selling little things I make, and I thought it would be super fun, you know? But now it's just... it's a disaster. I have my supplies literally everywhere. Like, my beads and my shipping mailers are somehow mixed up with my assignment notes. And the receipts! Oh my gosh, the receipts for the shop are just shoved into whatever bag or pocket I was using that day. And then I have due dates for my classes, and I try to write them down so I don't fail, but the papers and sticky notes just end up in these massive piles on my desk, on my bed, on the floor... just everywhere. 

I look at these giant piles of school stuff and shop stuff all mixed together and I just... I don't know what to do first. It's like I'll sit there and try to sort out a receipt, and then I'll see a notebook, and then I realize I don't even know where I put my homework... it's just completely overwhelming and I can't seem to figure out how to manage it all.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states they cannot get their schoolwork and shop organized, describing massive mixed piles of supplies, notes, and receipts, and an inability to prioritize tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions not knowing where they put their homework, indicating they lose items necessary for their schoolwork.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have problems with organization or attention like this when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, wow, yeah. Um, actually, it's funny you ask that because my mom was just talking about this the other day when I was complaining about how overwhelmed I am. She actually still has all these old notes and report cards from when I was in elementary school. Like, she kept a whole box of them, and they basically all say the exact same thing. 

The teachers were constantly writing to her about how I was literally always out of my seat. Like, I just couldn't stay glued to the chair during lessons, I'd always be wandering around or going to see what someone else was doing. And I was always, always talking before I was called on. I'd just blurt out the answers because, I don't know, I just couldn't wait for the teacher to finish asking the question or wait for someone else to raise their hand! It just felt like the words had to come out right that second or I would explode. 

And the notes also talked a lot about how I would just completely rush through group activities. Like, I actually understood the work, you know? I wasn't falling behind on the material itself, I totally got it, but I would just speed-run through the whole project because I wanted to be done and move on to the next thing. It would drive the other kids crazy because I wouldn't slow down to let them participate. So yeah, my mom looks at those notes now and says I've basically been going a million miles an hour since I was like, seven. I just always had to be moving or doing something, and I guess it's still like that now, just with my shop instead of a classroom.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient reports that in elementary school they were 'literally always out of my seat' and 'couldn't stay glued to the chair during lessons.'
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes themselves as 'going a million miles an hour' and states they 'always had to be moving or doing something.'
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they would 'blurt out the answers' and 'couldn't wait for the teacher to finish asking the question.'
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient mentions they couldn't wait for others to raise their hands and would rush through group activities without slowing down to let other kids participate.

turns.doctor_question: Do you currently have a hard time sustaining your attention when you're doing schoolwork or other tasks?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. It's honestly incredibly frustrating because I really do try. Like, when I'm in class, or especially when I'm watching these online video lectures for my business assignments—because I'm taking a few classes right now to try and help with the shop, you know, to learn about marketing and stuff—I always start out with the best intentions. 

I'll sit down, I'll have my notebook open, my pen ready, and for the first, I don't know, maybe three or four minutes, I'm totally locked in. I'm listening to the professor talk about whatever the topic is. But then... it's like my brain just completely pivots, and I don't even realize it's happening at first. Suddenly I'm thinking about these new resin charm designs I want to make, like wondering if I should add little holographic stars into the molds or if that would be too clunky. Or I'm brainstorming ideas for how to package my next batch of orders so they look cuter when people open them, going down this whole mental rabbit hole about tissue paper colors and custom stickers... 

And then, I don't know, I'll kind of snap back to reality and realize the video is still playing, or the professor is still talking, and I have absolutely no idea what they just said. I realize I missed literally half of what was said. And if it's a video, then I have to rewind it, which is just so annoying because a twenty-minute video ends up taking me an hour since I have to keep rewinding every time my brain decides to go think about charms again. And if it's a live class, well, I just completely missed it and have to hope I can figure it out later. It just feels impossible to keep my brain glued to the one thing it's actually supposed to be focusing on.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly confirms difficulty sustaining attention, noting that they can only focus on class or video lectures for a few minutes before losing track.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, such as brainstorming resin charm designs and packaging ideas during lectures.

turns.doctor_question: Do these attention and organization problems interfere with your schoolwork or daily life?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, it's honestly ruining everything right now. Like, it's not just a cute, quirky "oh I'm so messy" kind of thing, it's actually having massive consequences. 

With my classes, there are all these administrative hoops you have to jump through, right? And I was supposed to submit this academic progress form and complete a mandatory advising module online. I literally opened the tab for it like five different times over the course of a month, but I'd get distracted by an order that came in, or I'd start looking at the colors on the portal and think about a new logo design, and I just never actually did the module. And because of all this, because I completely missed those required steps for my program, I got this terrifying automated email last week saying my financial aid is now at risk of being suspended. Which is just... I mean, if I lose my financial aid, I literally cannot pay for these classes. And knowing that just makes me so anxious that I want to completely avoid looking at my inbox altogether, which obviously only makes the whole situation worse!

And then it's bleeding into my shop too, which breaks my heart because the shop is my favorite thing. I sometimes collaborate with other small creators—like, recently I was working with this girl who makes these beautiful crocheted bags, and we were supposed to do a special bundle launch where I made matching acrylic keychains to go on the zippers. But I kept losing track of our timeline. I would read her messages while I was doing something else, completely forget to reply, and then my supplies were such a disaster that I couldn't even find the right clasps to make the prototypes when I finally did remember. 

It's gotten to the point where the people I work with on shop projects have really started depending on me less. Like, she ended up just launching her bags without my keychains. She was super polite about it and said we could try again later, but I could totally tell she just couldn't rely on me to get my act together. She basically had to cut me out of the project so she wouldn't miss her own deadline. It just feels awful, you know? Like I'm letting absolutely everyone down, including myself, just because I can't keep a simple schedule straight or remember to click 'submit' on a form. I just talk and talk about all these big plans and then I completely drop the ball.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient failed to follow through on completing a mandatory advising module and academic progress form for school.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes losing track of project timelines, having disastrously disorganized supplies, and being unable to keep a schedule straight.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient could not find the necessary clasps for a project because their supplies were in such disarray.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient reports getting easily distracted from tasks by incoming orders or unrelated thoughts about logo designs.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient frequently forgets to reply to messages and forgets to click 'submit' on forms.

turns.doctor_question: Have you also had these attention or organization problems in other parts of your life, like at home, with chores, or with personal responsibilities?
turns.patient_response:
Um, well... I mean, I guess I'm not entirely sure what you mean by that? Like, I'm trying to think about my personal responsibilities and chores, and honestly, nothing really stands out to me as being a huge disaster in those specific areas. I mean, my room isn't spotless or anything, but whose is, right? I'll have piles of clothes on the chair, but I eventually put them away. I don't feel like I'm failing at basic life stuff the way I'm failing at school and the shop. 

Like, I make sure my cat is fed, I eventually get around to doing my laundry, even if it takes me a few days to fold it... it's not like the financial aid thing where my whole life is falling apart because I missed a deadline. I guess when it comes to just being at home, doing normal everyday stuff, I haven't really noticed any major issues with organization or attention. At least, not anything that feels like a real problem, you know? It's really just the school and the business stuff that's completely overwhelming me right now. So, yeah, I don't think I have those same kinds of problems with chores or whatever. I just... I don't know, it just doesn't feel like an issue at home.

symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly denies having problems with daily activities and chores, stating they feed their cat and do their laundry without major issues.

turns.doctor_question: Do these attention and organization problems also happen in more than one setting, like at home or in social situations, or mainly with school and your shop?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I mean, like I was kind of saying a second ago, it really is pretty much just the school and the shop. I definitely don't notice it in other places. 

Like, if you mean socially, with my friends or whatever? I don't have any problems there at all. I mean, we hang out all the time, and I don't zone out when they're talking or forget what we're doing. Like, just this past weekend, my friend Sarah and I went to the mall because she needed to find this very specific sage-green dress for her cousin's wedding—which has this whole 'enchanted forest' theme that is honestly a little much, but anyway—and I was completely focused on helping her find it. I wasn't getting distracted and wandering off or forgetting why we were in the store. 

And I don't really lose track of plans with my friends either. I guess because there's no real... organization required, you know? Like, there are no forms to fill out, no mandatory advising modules, no supply inventory to keep track of. We just text and say "hey, meet me at the coffee shop," and I go. Sometimes I might forget to text back immediately if my hands are literally covered in resin or something, but they know me, they just double-text me and it's fine. It doesn't cause these massive, bridge-burning disasters like it does with my shop collaborations. 

So, yeah, I really don't think it's an issue outside of my classes and the business. When I'm just living my normal life, hanging out with friends or just being at home, everything feels totally fine and normal. It's just those two specific areas where I feel like I'm completely drowning because there's so much to manage.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient confirms feeling like they are 'completely drowning because there's so much to manage' regarding school and their shop, indicating difficulty organizing tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient notes that forgetting to text back causes 'massive, bridge-burning disasters' with their shop collaborations.

turns.doctor_question: Before age 12, were you having these attention or organization problems regularly in more than one setting, like at school and at home?
turns.patient_response:
Um, before age 12? Gosh, that feels like a lifetime ago. But, um, yeah, actually. I mean, it wasn't the exact same kind of problems because obviously I didn't have a shop or financial aid forms back then, but... yeah. My mom actually still has this whole folder of my old elementary school stuff. She keeps everything, like every little drawing and report card. 

And, like, if you look at the notes from my teachers back in, like, second and third grade, it's honestly a little embarrassing. There are all these comments about how I was constantly out of my seat. Like, I just could not stay put during quiet time or when we were supposed to be working at our desks. I'd be up wandering around, looking at the classroom pet—we had a hamster named Barnaby, I think—or I'd be at the pencil sharpener for the fifth time. 

And I was always, always talking out of turn. Like, a teacher would ask a question, and before they even finished calling on someone, I would just blur out the answer. I just couldn't hold it in! It was like the thought was in my head and it had to escape my mouth immediately, no filter, no waiting. And group projects? Oh my gosh. I would just completely rush through everything. Like, I understood the material, I wasn't confused about the work itself, but I just wanted to get it done as fast as humanly possible. I would be practically vibrating with impatience, trying to hurry the other kids along, just slapping things together so we could move on to the next thing. So, yeah, I guess that kind of restless, impulsive stuff has been happening since I was really little, even if it looked a bit different back then.
